nuance.usage_note: Scholars of religion, linguistics and psychology use 'glossolalia' as a technical term. Believers more often say 'speaking in tongues'. Linguists generally note that it lacks the structure of a human language, while believers see it as a spiritual gift.

distinctions.note: Xenoglossy is speaking a real language one has never learned; glossolalia is typically unintelligible speech.
Gift of tongues is the religious term; glossolalia is the neutral scholarly term.
Gibberish is dismissive for meaningless speech; glossolalia is respectful and descriptive.

examples.everyday: My roommate is studying glossolalia for her anthropology thesis on Pentecostal worship.
examples.professional: The linguist's talk analyzed the sound patterns of glossolalia recorded in several churches.
examples.analytical: Whether glossolalia is a divine gift, a learned behavior, or a psychological phenomenon depends on the interpretive framework one adopts.

nuance.analogy: Glossolalia is like singing a melody without lyrics: the sound carries feeling more than literal meaning.
nuance.etymology: From Greek glōssa, 'tongue, language' + lalein, 'to speak'.
common_mistakes: Placing stress on 'gloss' instead of 'LAY'.
Pronouncing it 'glo-so-LAH-lee-a'.
Using it for any foreign language.
nuance.biblical_note: The word is not in the RSV, but it comes from the Greek glōssais lalein, 'to speak in tongues'. Acts 2:4 says the believers at Pentecost began to speak in other tongues. 1 Corinthians 14:2 says one who speaks in a tongue speaks to God, not people. 1 Corinthians 14:27-28 calls for interpretation or silence.

senses.definition: A friendly greeting to someone you already know.

core.definition: A friendly greeting you say to someone you already know when you meet them again.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SEE, and good gets a lighter secondary stress. In fast speech, to reduces to /tə/ and you to /jə/, so it sounds like 'good-tuh-SEE-yuh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and warm; it signals that you are glad to meet again.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this at work, in stores, at church or at the gym when they run into someone they know. A natural reply is 'Good to see you too' or simply 'You too!' It is friendly rather than intimate, and it is not used for first meetings, where 'Nice to meet you' is correct.

distinctions.note: Used only for first meetings; 'good to see you' is for people you already know.
More casual and playful, and it often implies a long gap since the last meeting.

examples.everyday: Hey Maria, good to see you! How's the family doing?
examples.professional: Good to see you, Kevin. Thanks for joining the call from the Denver office.
examples.analytical: When two colleagues meet after years apart, 'good to see you' expresses a social bond that the words themselves hardly need to carry.

nuance.analogy: Like a warm handshake in words: a quick sign that the connection still holds.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Good to meet you' to someone you already know, which sounds like you have forgotten them.
Stressing every word equally instead of putting the main stress on SEE.

conversation.text: Hey, good to see you! I didn't know you'd be here.
It was really good to see you yesterday. We should do it more often.
"Good to see you, man." "You too! How's the family?"

senses.definition: Blood, especially that from a wound when thickened due to exposure to the air.
Carnage, bloodshed, murder, violence.
Pictures and videos of graphic violence and human death.
A triangular piece of land where roads meet.
A small piece of land left unincorporated due to competing surveys or a surveying error.
The curved surface that lies between two close lines of longitude on a globe, or an equivalent section of a spherical or dome-shaped object in general.
A triangular or rhomboid piece of fabric, especially one forming part of a three-dimensional surface such as a sail or a skirt.
An elastic gusset for providing a snug fit in a shoe.
A projecting point.
A sign immediately adjacent to an exit from a roadway identifying it as an exit, optionally with the exit's identification number.
A charge, delineated by two inwardly curved lines, starting respectively from the middle base corner and one of the two chief corners and meeting in the fess point.
To pierce with a horn or tusk.
senses.example: The bull gored the matador.

senses.definition: To needle or wound the feelings of.
To cut into a triangular form.
To provide with a gore.
senses.example: to gore an apron

core.definition: Graphic violence, bloodshed or blood, especially as shown in movies, news or video games.

pronunciation.tip: Use the vowel of 'caught' and 'four', so /ɔɹ/, not the vowel of 'go'. Pronounce the r clearly, since American English is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes shocking, violent or disturbing content.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gore for violent movies, video games, crime reporting and horror stories, as in 'too much gore for me.' In casual talk, it can describe a gruesome accident. It is rarely a polite topic at dinner. The verb sense, to pierce with a horn, is mostly used in nature writing or about animals.

distinctions.note: Violence is the general act of harm; gore is the specific bloody, graphic detail of it.
Blood is the substance; gore often focuses on blood and wounds as a spectacle.

examples.everyday: I can't watch horror movies with that much gore, so I'll wait for the comedy.
examples.professional: Our content policy restricts gore in user uploads, and anything with graphic injury gets a warning label.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that gore in modern films can numb viewers rather than move them, because its shock fades with repetition.

nuance.analogy: Like a loud alarm that grabs attention: gore is the part of a violent story that the eye cannot ignore.
nuance.etymology: From Old English gor, meaning dirt or filth, later used for blood and slaughter.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing gore like 'go-r' with a long o, so it sounds like 'go.'
Confusing gore with gory and using them as interchangeable nouns and adjectives.

gore.etymology: From Middle English *gore*, *gor*, *gorre* (“mud, muck”), from Old English *gor* (“manure, dung, filth, muck, dirt”), from **gor*, from Proto-Germanic **gurą* (“half-digested stomach contents; faeces; manure”), from Proto-Indo-European **gʷʰer-* (“hot; warm”).

senses.definition: Proceeding or advancing by small, slow, regular steps or degrees.
senses.example: a gradual increase of knowledge; a gradual decline

senses.definition: An antiphon or responsory after the epistle, in the Mass, which was sung on the steps, or while the deacon ascended the steps.
A service book containing the musical portions of the Mass.

core.definition: Happening or developing slowly, in small steps or stages over a period of time, rather than suddenly.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the d and j blend into one sound as in 'judge'. The last syllable is a light schwa-l, not a separate 'ALL'.

nuance.connotation: positive or neutral. It describes a controlled, steady process and suggests less shock or risk than a sudden change.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'gradual' in both everyday talk and writing, usually with change, improvement, or transition. It is more often used as an adjective before a noun, while the adverb 'gradually' is more common in speech. Saying 'it got gradual' sounds wrong, so use 'it got better gradually'.

distinctions.note: Slow describes speed in general, while gradual emphasizes a change that happens in small, regular steps over time.
Incremental is more technical and business-focused, stressing measured additions, while gradual is the everyday word for steady change.

examples.everyday: The weather turned cold in such a gradual way that we barely noticed until we needed our jackets.
examples.professional: We are rolling out the new dashboard in gradual phases so that the support team can keep up.
examples.analytical: Burke argued that gradual reform preserves continuity better than revolutionary upheaval, because institutions can adapt without being broken.

nuance.analogy: A gradual change is like a slope rather than a cliff: you move up or down without a jolt.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin gradualis, meaning of steps, from Latin gradus, step.
common_mistakes: Using the adjective where the adverb is needed, as in 'it changed gradual' instead of 'it changed gradually'.
Pronouncing the middle sound as a hard g or a separate syllable in GRAJ-oo-ul.

gradual.etymology: From Medieval Latin *graduālis*, from Latin *gradus* (“step”), from Proto-Indo-European **gʰradʰ-*, **gʰredʰ-* (“to walk, go”).

senses.definition: An instinct or intuition; an immediate or basic feeling or reaction without a logical rationale.
senses.example: Don't think too hard about the answers to a personality test; just go with your gut feeling.

core.definition: A strong instinct or sense about something that comes without clear logical reasons.

pronunciation.tip: Stress GUT most strongly, and give feel-ing a lighter secondary stress. Link the words smoothly, and avoid stressing 'feel' too heavily as in 'feel-ING'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be positive when trusting instinct, but it may suggest a lack of evidence when used to justify a decision.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gut feeling in everyday talk and in business, for example 'I have a gut feeling this deal will fall through.' In professional settings people often add that they want evidence too. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I know what you mean' or 'Let's check the data first.'

distinctions.note: A hunch is a smaller, less serious guess; a gut feeling feels stronger and more physical.
Intuition is a more formal, general word for direct understanding without reasoning; gut feeling is more casual and emotional.

examples.everyday: I have a gut feeling the restaurant will be closed today, so let's call before we drive over.
examples.professional: I have a gut feeling this release will break the login flow, but let's run the regression tests before we decide.
examples.analytical: A gut feeling can be a useful signal, yet it is not evidence, and philosophers have long distinguished immediate conviction from justified belief.

nuance.analogy: A gut feeling is like a smoke alarm that goes off before you can see the fire: it may be right, but you should still check.
nuance.etymology: 'Gut' is from Old English 'guttas', the intestines, and was used for inner feeling; 'feeling' is from Old English 'felan', to perceive by touch.
common_mistakes: Using 'gut feelings' in the plural when speaking about one instinct; say 'a gut feeling'.
Saying 'a feeling of gut' instead of 'a gut feeling'.

conversation.text: I had a gut feeling something was wrong.
My gut feeling is that this candidate isn't the right fit.
Go with your gut feeling on the apartment.
My gut feeling says we should take the other road.
Trust your gut feeling about him.

senses.definition: The biceps femoris, semimembranosus, and semitendinosus muscles.
One of the great tendons situated in each side of the ham, or space back of the knee, and connected with the muscles of the back of the thigh.
To lame or disable by cutting the tendons of the ham or knee; to hough.
To cripple; to incapacitate; to disable.

core.definition: To cripple or severely limit someone or something, so that it cannot work or progress normally.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HAM. The second part is string with a flapped r sound, so say HAM-string as one smooth word.

nuance.connotation: negative. It suggests that someone or something is unfairly or deliberately weakened.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, hamstring is mostly used in the figurative sense of limiting someone's ability to act, especially in politics, business, or sports. People often say be hamstrung by a lack of money or be hamstrung by rules. The literal anatomical sense is much less common in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Hamper is a milder word for slowing progress. Hamstring suggests a stronger and more complete limitation, as if the ability to act has been cut.
Cripple is stronger and can carry a more personal or offensive tone. Hamstring is more common in discussions of policy or planning.

examples.everyday: My budget is hamstrung by the rent, so I can't really afford a vacation this year.
examples.professional: The unclear requirements hamstring our ability to plan the next release.
examples.analytical: Dogmatic commitments can hamstring a theologian's ability to read texts openly, because the conclusion is decided before the reading begins.

nuance.analogy: Hamstringing is like cutting a rope that helps a climber reach the top: the person is still there, but the means to move forward is cut.
nuance.etymology: From ham (back of the knee) and string (tendon), describing the tendons behind the knee.
common_mistakes: Using hamstring as a noun in place of the adjective hamstrung in phrases like be hamstring.
Saying hamstrang or other spelling variants instead of hamstrung for the past form.
Stressing the second syllable, as in ham-STRING.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Old Testament, hamstringing refers to cutting the tendons of an animal's hind legs, a practice that disabled horses used in war. The Hebrew verb behind it is 'aqar, meaning to hamstring or cut the tendons. Joshua 11:6 instructs Joshua to hamstring the horses of the northern coalition and burn their chariots. 2 Sam 8:4 reports that David hamstrung all but a hundred of the chariot horses he captured, leaving only enough for his own use.

senses.definition: Careful attention.
To mind; to regard with care; to take notice of; to attend to; to observe.

core.definition: As a noun, careful attention to something; as a verb, to pay careful attention to a warning, advice, or instruction.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is a long ē, so it rhymes with 'need' and 'speed'. Do not shorten it to the vowel in 'hid'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it usually signals wise attentiveness, though 'heed' in warnings can be stern.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use 'heed' in the phrase 'heed a warning' or 'take heed', often in news, safety notices, or stern advice. In casual speech they might say 'pay attention to' or 'listen to' instead. 'Take heed' sounds slightly formal or old-fashioned, so use it carefully in conversation.

distinctions.note: Notice means to become aware of something, while heed means to act on it or take it seriously.
Attend to is more general and neutral, covering handling tasks or paying attention, while heed is specifically about taking a warning or advice seriously.

examples.everyday: If the weather app says a storm is coming, you should heed it and stay off the lake.
examples.professional: Our team needs to heed the security alert from IT and update every password by Friday.
examples.analytical: The prophet's listeners failed to heed his warning, and the author suggests their failure was a failure of attention rather than of knowledge.

nuance.analogy: To heed a warning is like a driver seeing a red light and actually stopping, instead of just noticing it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hēdan, meaning 'to take care of, to guard'.
common_mistakes: Using 'heed to' instead of 'heed' alone, as in 'heed to the advice'; 'heed' takes a direct object.
Confusing 'heed' with 'head', which is pronounced the same way but is a different word meaning the top of the body.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, heeding means giving careful attention to God's word and commands, so that one's life is shaped by them. Hebrews 2:1 urges readers to pay closer attention to what they have heard, lest they drift away from it. Proverbs 4:20 asks the listener to attend closely to the teacher's words, and the Hebrew verb for attending there is the same root used in urging a child to keep wisdom in view. The Greek verb prosechō in Hebrews 2:1 carries the sense of giving full mind and concern to something.

heed.etymology: From Middle English *heden*, from Old English *hēdan* (“to heed, take care, observe, attend, guard, take charge, take possession, receive”), from **hōdijan* (“to heed, guard”), of contested origin.

senses.definition: A doctrine held by a member of a religion at variance or conflict with established religious beliefs.
A controversial or unorthodox opinion held by a member of a group, as in politics, philosophy or science.

core.definition: A belief or teaching that contradicts the core doctrine of a religion, especially Christianity; more broadly, any opinion that defies accepted orthodoxy in a field.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, which rhymes with 'air' in American English. The middle syllable is a weak schwa, so do not say 'hee-ruh-see'.

nuance.connotation: Negative in religious contexts, since it implies a condemned error. Used playfully or admiringly for bold ideas that challenge a field.
nuance.usage_note: In theology, heresy means a serious departure from doctrine the church holds essential, not mere disagreement. Americans also use it jokingly, as in 'Putting ketchup on steak is heresy!' The person is a heretic, and the adjective is heretical.

distinctions.note: A schism is a split in church unity or communion, while heresy is a false teaching; the two can occur separately.
Apostasy is abandoning the faith altogether, while heresy is distorting it from within.
Blasphemy is irreverent speech or action against God or sacred things, not necessarily a doctrinal error.

examples.everyday: My uncle thinks pineapple on pizza is heresy, and he won't hear otherwise.
examples.professional: Suggesting we skip code review used to be heresy here, but now we're willing to test it.
examples.analytical: Early councils defined orthodoxy largely in response to heresies such as Arianism, which denied the full divinity of the Son.

nuance.analogy: Heresy is like a wrong note played so insistently that it changes the melody everyone else is singing.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hairesis, 'choice, a taking,' later 'a school of thought,' through Latin haeresis.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'HEER-uh-see' or 'huh-REE-see'.
Confusing heresy with heretic; heresy is the belief, the heretic is the person.
Treating it as a synonym for any disagreement, when it implies a breach of established doctrine.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word hairesis appears in the New Testament meaning a party or faction (Acts 5:17, of the Sadducees) and divisive opinions. In 1 Corinthians 11:19 Paul says factions must exist among the Corinthians so the genuine may be recognized. In 2 Peter 2:1 false teachers secretly bring in destructive opinions, even denying the Master who bought them. Titus 3:10 tells the church to warn a factious person and then have nothing to do with him.

traditions.view: Heresy is a departure from the faith defined by the ecumenical councils and the Fathers. The Church judges it conciliarly, and the seven councils set the standard.

Heresy is the obstinate denial or doubt, after baptism, of a truth that must be believed with divine and Catholic faith. The Magisterium decides what counts as heresy, and canon law treats it as a grave offense.

Heresy is generally a teaching that contradicts Scripture's essential gospel truths, such as the Trinity or Christ's deity. Protestants differ on what counts as essential, and many confessions (Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican) cite the early creeds as a norm under Scripture.

heresy.etymology: From Middle English *heresie* (*enm:heresie* + *-esy*), from Old French *heresie* (modern *hérésie*), from Latin *haeresis*, from Ancient Greek *αἵρεσις* (“choice, system of principles”), from *αἱρέομαι* (“to take for oneself, to choose”), the middle voice…

core.definition: A man in the Bible, son of Perez and grandson of Judah, who is an ancestor of David and of Jesus.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HEZ, and make the r clearly American. The final vowel is the cot vowel, like 'hon'.

nuance.connotation: neutral; a name from the Bible with no particular charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans know Hezron from Bible study and genealogies, especially Ruth and Matthew. It is rarely used outside Christian or biblical contexts. Some Americans may confuse it with Hezekiah, so be precise when discussing either.

distinctions.note: Hezron is an ancestor in a genealogy of Judah, while Hezekiah is a king of Judah with a long narrative in Kings and Chronicles.

examples.everyday: In the Bible reading, the family tree goes Perez, then Hezron, then Ram, and it's easy to lose track.
examples.professional: When I teach Ruth, I point out that Hezron appears in the genealogy that links Judah to King David.
examples.analytical: The genealogy of Ruth 4 traces David's line through Hezron, which links the royal house to the tribe of Judah.

nuance.analogy: Hezron is like a link in a long chain of ancestors: a name that carries the family forward from Judah to David.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Ḥeṣrōn; the meaning of the name is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing Hezron with Hezekiah, since they start the same way.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: Hezron (Hebrew Ḥeṣrōn) is a son of Perez and grandson of Judah, and he appears in the genealogies that lead to David. Genesis 46:12 lists him among Judah's descendants who went down to Egypt with Jacob. Ruth 4:18-19 gives the line from Perez through Hezron and Ram to David. Matthew 1:3 includes Hezron in the genealogy of Jesus, which links Jesus to the line of Judah.

senses.definition: Lacking liquidity.
senses.example: illiquid assets

senses.definition: Not readily converted into cash.
senses.example: illiquid assets

senses.definition: Having substantial assets but with most of them being of types not readily converted into cash (thus, not having much ready money).
senses.example: illiquid millionaires

core.definition: Hard to turn quickly into cash without losing value, such as certain investments or property.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, LIK. The 'qu' is pronounced 'kw', and the final 'id' is a short 'id', like 'kid'.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a precise financial term, sometimes used as a warning about risk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'illiquid' in finance and business, such as 'illiquid assets' or 'illiquid market'. It is not used in everyday talk; people say 'I don't have cash' or 'I can't sell it quickly'. Ask a financial advisor about an illiquid investment before you buy.

distinctions.note: 'Insolvent' means unable to pay debts at all; 'illiquid' means having assets that are hard to sell quickly, which may still be worth more than the debts.
'Poor' describes low wealth overall; 'illiquid' describes wealth tied up in assets that can't be sold quickly.

examples.everyday: I own a lot of land, but it's so illiquid that I can't pay the bill this month.
examples.professional: Our fund holds several illiquid assets, so we need a plan for redemptions during downturns.
examples.analytical: Keynes's analysis implies that a market becomes illiquid when investors lose confidence in any price.

nuance.analogy: Illiquid assets are like a painting in a locked gallery: it has value, but you can't get it into your wallet quickly.
nuance.etymology: From 'il-' (not) plus 'liquid', from Latin 'liquidus', meaning 'flowing' or 'clear'.
common_mistakes: Using 'illiquid' to mean 'broke' or 'poor' in everyday talk.
Confusing it with 'illicit' or 'illegible' because of similar spelling.

senses.definition: To drink (used frequently of alcoholic beverages).
To take in; absorb.
senses.example: to imbibe knowledge

core.definition: To drink, especially alcohol; also to take in ideas, feelings, or information gradually.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the single syllable BYBE, with a long i like the word 'eye'. Keep the final b as a clear stop rather than reducing it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly playful: it sounds refined or old-fashioned when used for drinking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'drink' for everyday beverages. 'Imbibe' suggests a refined or playful tone, as in a cocktail menu or a toast. It is also used figuratively for absorbing ideas, as in 'imbibe the local culture'. Its humorous edge makes it less likely in serious conversation.

distinctions.note: Drink is the plain everyday verb; imbibe is more formal or playful and can mean absorbing ideas, not just liquid.
Absorb is neutral for taking in information or liquid; imbibe is more literary and suggests drinking something in gradually.

examples.everyday: We went to a rooftop bar and imbibed a few cocktails before dinner.
examples.professional: New hires imbibe our product philosophy during onboarding, so customers hear one consistent voice.
examples.analytical: Young Augustine imbibed the rhetoric of Cicero, and that love of eloquence shaped his later theology.

nuance.analogy: To imbibe is like a sponge taking in water: the drink or the idea soaks in deeply.
nuance.etymology: From Latin imbibere 'to drink in', from in- 'in' plus bibere 'to drink'.
common_mistakes: Using imbibe in casual speech for ordinary drinking; it sounds stylized.
Stressing the first syllable; it is im-BYBE.

imbibe.etymology: From Middle English *imbiben*, from Latin *imbibō*, from *im-* + *bibō* (“to drink”) (whence also *beverage*), from Proto-Italic **pibō*, from Proto-Indo-European **peh₃-*, whence also *potable*, *potion*.

senses.definition: The quality of being immediate, of happening right away.
Lack of mediation; directness.
Immediate awareness or apprehension.

core.definition: The quality of happening right away, or of feeling direct, close, and urgent.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MEE, and the word has two separate ee sounds before the reduced vowel. Learners often reduce the first ee or add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can suggest urgency, directness, or a valued sense of closeness, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use immediacy in writing about media, art, politics, and design, such as the immediacy of live video. In everyday speech they would more often say how fast something happens or how urgent it feels. The word is most natural when discussing an effect rather than just a timing.

distinctions.note: Urgency is the need for quick action, while immediacy is the quality of being direct or present, which may or may not feel urgent.
Promptness refers to acting on time, usually in a practical sense, while immediacy describes the felt quality of being right here and now.

examples.everyday: I like watching the game live because there's an immediacy to it that you just don't get from a recap.
examples.professional: Dashboards give the team immediacy in incident response, but we need to verify the data before we act on it.
examples.analytical: Husserl's phenomenology aims at the immediacy of experience, the way things present themselves before theory interprets them.

nuance.analogy: Like touching a hot stove versus reading about burns: the experience has an immediacy that no description can match.
nuance.etymology: From immediate plus the suffix -acy, from Medieval Latin immediatus, meaning without an intervening thing.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable instead of the second.
Confusing immediacy with immediately, which is an adverb.
Using immediacy to mean the same thing as speed, when it often refers to directness or presence.

senses.definition: Filled with intense emotion or passion; fervent.

core.definition: Filled with intense feeling; passionate and fervent, especially when pleading for a cause or speaking about something you care about deeply.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, PASH, and the final -ed is a reduced vowel plus d, so it sounds like und. The ss is a sharp sh sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; admired in speeches, pleas, and arguments, though it can sound overwrought in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for speeches, appeals, debates, and writing, as in an impassioned plea. In casual talk people more often say passionate or worked up. It rarely describes someone's mood in small talk. A natural reply to an impassioned speech is simply agreement or a question about the cause.

distinctions.note: Passionate is the everyday word and can describe a person or a hobby; impassioned is more formal and is usually used about speech, writing, or pleas.
Fervent suggests warm, sincere devotion, often religious or loyal; impassioned highlights emotion expressed through words.

examples.everyday: My sister gave an impassioned speech at dinner about why we should adopt a dog.
examples.professional: Maria made an impassioned case in the meeting for funding the new data pipeline.
examples.analytical: Her impassioned defense of the prophets rests on an appeal to conscience rather than to authority.

nuance.analogy: A speech that burns like a campfire rather than a candle.
nuance.etymology: From impassion, from Latin passio 'suffering', from pati 'to suffer'.
common_mistakes: Using impassioned for a casual mood; 'I am impassioned about soccer' sounds stiff, so say passionate.
Stressing the wrong syllable as im-PASS-ee-und.

senses.definition: Not practicable; impossible or difficult in practice.
Impassable.

core.definition: Impossible or too difficult to carry out in real life; not feasible.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, PRAK. The ending 'able' is reduced to 'buhl', and the t in 'practicable' is a clear t, not a flap, because it is stressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a plan or idea that cannot be carried out in practice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say impractical or not feasible instead. Impracticable is more often found in legal or older writing, and it can sound stiff in conversation. Use it when you want a precise, formal word for something that cannot be done in practice.

distinctions.note: Impractical is the everyday American word meaning not sensible or workable; impracticable is stronger and means it cannot be done at all.
Unfeasible is a neutral term for not doable, often used in planning; impracticable is more formal and literary.

examples.everyday: Driving to the airport at rush hour would be impracticable, so let's take the train.
examples.professional: Migrating the entire legacy database in one sprint is impracticable given our current staffing.
examples.analytical: Kant argues that a universal moral law is impracticable if it demands what human nature cannot sustain.

nuance.analogy: An impracticable plan is like a bridge drawn on a map across a canyon with no materials to build it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin impracticabilis, from in- (not) and practicabilis (feasible, workable), from practicare (to practice).
common_mistakes: Using impracticable in casual talk when impractical sounds more natural.
Confusing impracticable (cannot be done) with impractical (not sensible).

senses.definition: Someone or thing who lives in a place.
A possible value for a type.
Resident.

core.definition: A person or animal that lives in a particular place. In computing, a possible value of a type set, such as an element of a data type.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HAB. The last two syllables are reduced to 'tunt', with the 'a' in 'ant' lightly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is more formal than 'resident' or 'local' and is often used in news and geography.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'inhabitant' mostly in writing about cities, countries, or history, such as 'the inhabitants of the village.' In everyday speech, 'resident' or 'people who live here' is more natural. In technical contexts such as computing or mathematics, 'inhabitant' means a member of a set or a possible value.

distinctions.note: 'Resident' is the everyday word for a person living somewhere, often with legal or official sense. 'Inhabitant' is more literary and historical.
'Native' emphasizes being born in a place or its original people. 'Inhabitant' only says someone lives there.

examples.everyday: The inhabitants of our street all know each other, so we always help when someone is moving.
examples.professional: In the data model, each inhabitant of the enumeration type must be one of the three approved status codes.
examples.analytical: Who counts as an inhabitant of a city is a question that shapes political representation and census policy.

nuance.analogy: Think of a town as a house. The inhabitants are the people living in its rooms, so each one belongs to that house in a particular way.
nuance.etymology: From Latin inhabitans, present participle of inhabitare 'to dwell in'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as 'in-hab-I-tant'.
Using 'inhabitant' as casual slang for a visitor or neighbor; it sounds formal.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew yoshev (one who dwells or sits) and the Greek katoikos (dweller) are behind the idea of inhabitants. Psalm 24:1 in the RSV says the world and those who dwell therein belong to the LORD. The same idea appears in Genesis, where God's people settle in lands given to them.

inhabitant.etymology: From Middle English *inhabitantes* and *inhabitaunt*, from Old French *inhabitant*, from Latin *inhabitāns*, present participle of *inhabitō* (“to inhabit”), from *in-* (“in”) + *habitō* (“to dwell”) (frequentative of *habeō* (“to hold”), from…

senses.definition: Characterized by iniquity (“deviation from what is right”).
Morally objectionable; sinful, wicked.
Grossly unfair or unjust.

core.definition: Morally wrong and grossly unfair; sinful or wicked in a way that causes injustice.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NIK, the second syllable. The -kw- is a clear 'kw' sound, and the ending is a light 'tus'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It condemns a system, law, or act as unjust and morally wrong.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use iniquitous in formal commentary, political writing, sermons, and literary prose about unfair laws, taxes, or institutions. It is strong, so save it for serious injustice. In everyday speech, people say unfair or outrageous.

distinctions.note: Unfair is everyday and mild; iniquitous is a much stronger word implying moral wrong and serious injustice.
Wicked describes evil in a person; iniquitous often describes an unjust system or practice.

examples.everyday: Charging people extra just because they're poor is iniquitous, and I told my dad so.
examples.professional: The contract's hidden fees are iniquitous, and legal should review it before we sign.
examples.analytical: Rawls argues that a social order that rewards arbitrary advantage is iniquitous, even when it is stable.

nuance.analogy: Like a scale that is rigged from the start, so the outcome is unjust before anyone is weighed.
nuance.etymology: From Latin iniquitas, from iniquus 'unequal, unjust', from in- 'not' plus aequus 'equal'.
common_mistakes: Using iniquitous for minor annoyances, which sounds exaggerated.
Confusing the adjective iniquitous with the noun iniquity.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the idea is avon, meaning crookedness, guilt, or its punishment; the Greek is anomia or adikia. The RSV uses iniquity for these. Psalm 51:2 asks God to wash the psalmist from his iniquity. Exodus 34:7 describes God as forgiving iniquity and transgression. Isaiah 53:6 says the Lord laid on the servant the iniquity of us all.

senses.definition: The production of an instance, example, or specific application of a general classification, principle, theory, etc.
Something resulting from the act of instantiating; an instance.
A creation of an instance of some class or template.

core.definition: The act of creating a specific instance of a general class, principle, or template, or the instance that results from that act.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on AY, the fourth syllable, and the ending 'shun' is reduced. Learners often stress the 'stan' syllable or say 'shee-ay' as two full syllables, so keep the 'shee' light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is precise and mainly used in specialist writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'instantiation' mostly in logic, computer science, and philosophy to describe the act or result of making a concrete example from a general type. In casual speech it sounds jargony, so 'an example of' or 'a specific case of' is more natural. In programming, people also say 'object creation' for the same idea.

distinctions.note: An instance is the concrete example itself, while instantiation is the act or process of producing that example from a general type.
An example is a general word for something illustrating a point, while instantiation is a technical term for making a specific case from a general template.
Realization means making something real or achieving a goal, while instantiation specifically means producing a concrete case of a general abstraction.

examples.everyday: This family dinner is a small instantiation of the tradition we've kept since my grandmother's time.
examples.professional: In the Python code, each object is an instantiation of the class, so changes to one do not affect the others.
examples.analytical: Every particular law is an instantiation of a more general principle, and the question is how far the principle determines the case.

nuance.analogy: Like a mold and the figurine cast from it: the mold is the general form, and each figurine is a concrete instantiation.
nuance.etymology: From 'instantiate', from 'instance', from Latin instantia 'presence, urgency', with the noun suffix '-ation'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'instantiation' with 'instance'; the instance is the result, and instantiation is the process.
Stressing the 'stan' syllable instead of the 'ay' syllable.

instantiation.etymology: A coinage of the twentieth century, from *instantiate* + *-ion*, itself coined in 1946 from *instance* + *-ate*.

senses.definition: Stopping and starting, occurring, or presenting at intervals; coming after a particular time span.
senses.example: The day was cloudy with intermittent rain.

senses.definition: Existing only for certain seasons; that is, being dry for part of the year.
senses.example: The area has many intermittent lakes and streams.

senses.definition: An intermittent fever or disease.

core.definition: Happening or stopping and starting at irregular intervals, rather than continuously.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MIT. The last two syllables are reduced, so the t is often a flap and the n is syllabic; say MIT-nt, not mit-ee-nt.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: describes a pattern without judging it.
nuance.usage_note: Common in everyday speech and technical writing for signals, pain, rain, or internet connections that come and go. Americans often say on and off to sound more casual. It is equally natural in writing and conversation.

distinctions.note: Sporadic suggests random, scattered occurrences; intermittent suggests a stop-start pattern over time.
Periodic means recurring at regular intervals; intermittent may be irregular.

examples.everyday: The wifi has been intermittent all morning, so I can't stream anything.
examples.professional: The server throws intermittent timeouts, so we need logs from the failed requests.
examples.analytical: An intermittent reinforcement schedule produces more persistent behavior than continuous reward does.

nuance.analogy: Like a turn signal that blinks on and off rather than staying lit.
nuance.etymology: From Latin intermittere 'to leave off between', from inter- 'between' plus mittere 'to send, let go'.
common_mistakes: Confusing intermittent with intermediate, which means between two stages or levels.
Stressing the second syllable, as in in-ter-MIT-ee-nt, or giving the ending a full vowel.

intermittent.etymology: From Middle French *intermittent*, from Latin *intermittens* (“sending between”), from prefix *inter-* (“among, on”) + *mittens* (“sending”), from *mittere* (“to send”).

senses.definition: The rise and fall of the voice in speaking.
Emotive stress used to increase the power of delivery in speech.
A sound made by, or resembling that made by, a musical instrument.
Singing or playing in good tune or otherwise.
senses.example: Her intonation was false.

senses.definition: Reciting in a musical prolonged tone; intonating or singing of the opening phrase of a plain-chant, psalm, or canticle by a single voice, as of a priest.

core.definition: The rise and fall of the voice in speech, which can signal questions, emotion, or emphasis.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NAY, the third syllable, and the final -tion is 'shun'. The middle vowels are weak, so do not pronounce them as clear 'oo' or 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: neutral; it is a descriptive term without positive or negative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use intonation in discussions of speaking, language learning, and communication. A rising intonation at the end of a statement makes it sound like a question. In everyday talk, people more often say 'tone' or 'the way you said it.'

distinctions.note: Tone is broader and includes emotional attitude; intonation is specifically the pitch pattern of speech.
An accent is how sounds are pronounced in a region; intonation is the melody of a phrase.
Stress is emphasis on a syllable within a word; intonation is pitch movement across a whole sentence.

examples.everyday: Your intonation goes up at the end, so people think you're asking a question.
examples.professional: In presentations, a flat intonation can make the most important numbers disappear.
examples.analytical: In English, intonation can distinguish a question from a statement without any change in word order.

nuance.analogy: Intonation is like the melody of a song, while the words are the lyrics.
nuance.etymology: From Latin intonare 'to sound aloud', from in- 'into' + tonare 'to thunder'.
common_mistakes: Confusing intonation with stress; intonation is pitch across a phrase, while stress is emphasis on a syllable.
Using intonation as a countable noun for a single pitch movement; it is usually uncountable.

intonation.etymology: From French *intonation*, from Medieval Latin *intonatio*, from *intonō* + *tiō*.

senses.definition: Not tractable; not able to be managed, controlled, governed or directed.
Not able to be solved in polynomial time; too difficult to attempt to solve.
Difficult to deal with, solve, or manage.
Stubborn; obstinate.
Difficult to treat (of a medical condition).

core.definition: Very hard to solve, control or change; stubbornly unmanageable. In computing, a problem too hard to solve efficiently.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TRAK, not the first. The t before r is not flapped, and the final -able is reduced to a light 'buhl' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes problems, conflicts or people that resist every effort to fix or manage them, and it sounds serious rather than casual.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use intractable most often for stubborn problems, such as an intractable conflict, an intractable disease, or a budget deficit that seems intractable. In casual speech people more often say hard to fix or impossible to deal with. In data science and computer science, intractable is a precise term for problems whose solution time grows faster than any polynomial in the input size.

distinctions.note: Stubborn describes a person's will; intractable describes a problem, situation or a person who is very hard to manage, and it is stronger and more formal.
Difficult is everyday and neutral in strength; intractable implies the difficulty cannot be overcome with ordinary effort.
Unsolvable means no solution exists; intractable means a solution exists in principle but is too hard to find in practice.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's dispute over the fence has become intractable, and nobody on the block wants to talk about it anymore.
examples.professional: The scheduling issue turned out to be an intractable problem, so we agreed to use an approximation instead of an exact solution.
examples.analytical: Some moral disagreements appear intractable because each side rests its claims on premises the other side does not accept.

nuance.analogy: An intractable problem is like a knot pulled tighter the harder you tug; the more force you apply, the worse it gets.
nuance.etymology: From Latin in- (not) and tractabilis (manageable), from trahere, to draw or drag.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as IN-trak-tuh-bul instead of in-TRAK-tuh-buhl.
Using intractable for a simple, merely inconvenient problem; it implies serious difficulty.
Saying intractable with a hard t before r; the t is pronounced clearly, not flapped.

senses.definition: Such that it cannot be repaired.

core.definition: In a way that cannot be repaired, restored, or fixed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first 'REP' syllable, and say the American 'r' clearly. The ending is 'uh-blee', with a weak middle syllable and a long 'ee' at the end.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It emphasizes permanent, serious harm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adverb with verbs like 'damaged', 'harmed', or 'broken' to show that the damage is permanent. It is common in news reports, legal writing, and serious conversation. In casual speech people often say 'totally ruined' or 'can't be fixed', but 'irreparably' is natural when the seriousness matters.

distinctions.note: Irremediably is less common and suggests that no cure or correction is possible, while irreparably suggests that something broken cannot be restored.
Permanently means lasting forever, but irreparably adds the sense that the thing is broken beyond any way of restoring it.

examples.everyday: My old laptop got soaked in the rain, and it's irreparably broken now.
examples.professional: The outage irreparably damaged our customer trust, so we need a full postmortem before we restore the service.
examples.analytical: Tragedy, on this reading, depicts a world in which a single choice can irreparably alter the moral order.

nuance.analogy: Once a glass shatters into pieces, it has been irreparably broken, because no glue can make it whole again.
nuance.etymology: From irreparable plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Placing the stress on the last syllable, saying 'ih-reh-PAR-uh-blee' instead of 'ih-REP-uh-blee'.
Confusing it with 'irrevocably', which means that a decision cannot be reversed rather than that damage cannot be repaired.

senses.definition: Reassuring someone.

core.definition: A reassuring way to tell someone that a problem or situation will turn out fine in the end.

pronunciation.tip: It'll is pronounced like IT-uhl with the t often flapped or dropped, and okay stresses the second syllable, oh-KAY. Phrases like this link smoothly, so it'll be sounds like it-uhl-bee.

nuance.connotation: positive and comforting
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this to friends, family and coworkers when someone is worried, sad or stressed. It is very natural and warm, and it can be used in serious situations too. A natural reply is 'Thanks, I hope so' or 'I really appreciate that.' Avoid saying it to dismiss a serious concern, because it can then sound careless.

distinctions.note: Fine is a little more general and often used for minor problems, while okay is slightly more casual and focused on the outcome being acceptable.
Don't worry is a direct instruction to stop feeling anxious, whereas it'll be okay is a prediction that offers reassurance.

antonyms: it's not going to be okay

examples.everyday: You missed the bus, but don't stress, it'll be okay and we can grab a ride.
examples.professional: The server outage is annoying, but it'll be okay once the team restores the backup.
examples.analytical: To say it'll be okay is a promise about the future, and philosophers would ask what evidence supports such a promise.

nuance.analogy: Like a warm blanket on a cold night: it does not remove the cold, but it makes it bearable.
common_mistakes: Saying 'It will be okey' with a spelling-based pronunciation; the word is OH-KAY.
Using it to dismiss someone's serious feelings, which can sound unkind.

conversation.text: Don't cry, sweetie. It'll be okay.
"I'm so worried about the surgery." "It'll be okay. The doctors are great."
We'll find another apartment. It'll be okay.

senses.definition: A mechanical device or utensil used for lifting.
senses.example: She used a jack to lift her car and changed the tire.

senses.definition: A tool used in manual production of glass objects (like bottles or wine glasses).
A non-tool object or thing.
senses.example: You haven't done jack. Get up and get this room cleaned up right now!

senses.definition: A mechanical device used to raise and (temporarily) support a heavy object, now especially to lift one side of a motor vehicle when (e.g.) changing a tire.
senses.example: She used a jack to lift her car and changed the tire.

senses.definition: A coarse medieval coat of defense, especially one made of leather.
senses.example: jack of plate

senses.definition: A man. A sailor.
A name applied to a hypothetical or typical man.
A man, a fellow; a typical man; men in general.
A sailor.
A policeman or detective; a military policeman.
A lumberjack.
A device for turning a spit; a smokejack or roasting jack.
Each of a series of blocks in a harpsichord or the earlier virginal, communicating the action of the key to the quill; sometime also, a hopper in a modern piano.
A device used to hold a boot by the heel, to assist in removing the boot.
Any of various levers for raising or lowering the sinkers which push the loops down on the needles in a knitting machine or stocking frame.
A switch for a jack plug, a jackknife switch; a socket used to connect a device to a circuit, network etc.
senses.example: telephone jack

senses.definition: The lowest court card in a deck of standard playing cards, ranking between the 10 and queen, with an image of a knave or pageboy on it.
A small, typically white, ball used as the target ball in bowls; a jack-ball.
A small, six-pointed playing piece used in the game of jacks.
A torch or other light used in hunting to attract or dazzle game at night.
Money, cash.
A strong alcoholic liquor, especially home-distilled or illicit.
Nothing, not anything, jack shit.
senses.example: You haven't done jack. Get up and get this room cleaned up right now!

senses.definition: A smooth often ovoid large gravel or small cobble in a natural water course.
A plant or animal.
A pike, especially when young.
A male ass, especially when kept for breeding.
Any of the marine fish in the family Carangidae.
A jackrabbit.
A bocaccio (Sebastes paucispinis), a large California rockfish.
White mango (Mangifera caesia). (See #Etymology 4.)
A Jack-in-the-pulpit (Arisaema), often capitalized Jack.
Spadix of a plant (also capitalized Jack).

Any member of species of the genus Emex, also considered synonymous to Rumex, if not then containing two species lesser jack and little jack for Emex spinosa syn. Rumex spinosus, Australian English three-corner jack and prickly jack for Emex australis syn. Rumex hypogaeus.
A jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus, syn. Artocarpus integrifolia).
White mango (Mangifera caesia) of fruit-bearing plants.
A small ship's flag used as a signal or identifying device; a small flag flown at the bow of the vessel.
The eleventh batsman to come to the crease in an innings.
A home run.
A manual laborer.
A wedge for separating rocks rent by blasting.
A pitcher or other vessel for holding liquid, especially alcoholic drink; a black-jack.
A jackcrosstree.
To physically raise using a jack.
senses.example: He jacked the car so that he could replace the brake pads.

senses.definition: To raise or increase.
senses.example: If you want to jack your stats you just write off failures as invalid results.

senses.definition: To increase the potency of an alcoholic beverage similarly to distillation by chilling it to below the freezing point of water, removing the water ice crystals that form, and leaving the still-liquid alcoholic portion.
To steal (something), typically an automobile; to rob (someone).
senses.example: Someone jacked my car last night!

senses.definition: To dance by moving the torso forward and backward in a rippling motion.
To jack off, to masturbate.
To fight.
To jerk or move by jerking; to remove or move (something).
To hit (the ball) hard; especially, to hit (the ball) out of the field, producing a home run.
Tired, disillusioned; fed up (with).

core.definition: A hand-operated device that lifts a heavy object, such as a car, a few inches off the ground so you can change a tire.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short 'a' as in 'cat' and a hard 'j' sound. Americans say the word as one syllable with a clear final 'k'.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: In American English, jack most often means a car jack for lifting a vehicle to change a flat tire. In a conversation about a car, someone might say 'Did you bring the jack?' Note that in some contexts, jack also means a playing card or a plug connector.

distinctions.note: Lift is the general action; jack is a specific tool or the act of raising something with one.
Hoist usually means raising heavy goods with ropes or machinery, while jack suggests a compact mechanical lift.

examples.everyday: Can you hand me the jack? I need to change this flat tire.
examples.professional: The maintenance team checked the hydraulic jack before lifting the equipment.
examples.analytical: The jack is a simple machine that multiplies force, allowing a small effort to lift a large load.

nuance.analogy: A jack is like a small lever that lets you lift a heavy weight with less effort.
nuance.etymology: From the proper name Jack, used as a nickname for John, applied to many common tools.
common_mistakes: Using 'jack' to mean 'lift the car' without the verb 'jack up'.
Confusing 'jack' with 'jacket' in casual speech.

jack.etymology: Middle English *jakke*, from Anglo-Norman *jacke*, Middle French *jaque*, *jacque*, from *jacques* (“peasant”), from the proper name *Jacques*.

conversation.text: There's a jack and a spare tire in the trunk.
Jack up the car before you take the wheel off.
Put the jack under the metal frame, not the plastic.

core.definition: The name of two kings in the Bible: a king of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat, and a king of Israel, son of Ahab, who was killed by Jehu.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on HOR, the second syllable, and the r is pronounced clearly because General American is rhotic. The last syllable is a weak schwa.

nuance.connotation: neutral as a name; the two kings are judged negatively in the biblical narrative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this name in Bible study and historical discussion, and context shows which king is meant. The name is written with a capital letter and needs no article. When the reference is ambiguous, speakers often add 'of Judah' or 'of Israel'.

distinctions.note: Joram is the shorter form of the same name, and some English Bibles use Joram for the king of Israel. The two spellings refer to the same person.

examples.everyday: When I read about Jehoram, I got confused because there are two kings with that name.
examples.professional: In the lesson plan, I labeled each Jehoram by kingdom so the students would not mix them up.
examples.analytical: The double use of the name Jehoram in the historical books produces a deliberate parallel between the two kingdoms' failures.

nuance.analogy: Like two people with the same name in the same family, so you have to add a label to tell them apart.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew Yəhôrām, meaning 'Yahweh is exalted' or 'Yahweh is high'.
common_mistakes: Assuming there is only one Jehoram in the Bible.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'hor-AM' instead of 'HOR-um'.
nuance.biblical_note: Two kings bear the name Jehoram in the Old Testament. The king of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat, married Athaliah and led the kingdom into idolatry. The king of Israel, son of Ahab, was killed by Jehu in the field at Jezreel, as recorded in 2 Kings 9.

senses.definition: To put in jeopardy, to threaten.
senses.example: After having an affair with a junior, her chances of promotion were seriously jeopardized.

core.definition: To put something valuable or someone at risk of harm, loss or failure.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, JEP. The middle syllable is a reduced 'er' in American speech, not a full 'ar'. Final -ize is pronounced like 'dyze'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it describes a threat or risk to something important.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use jeopardize in news, business, medicine, politics and everyday talk about risks, such as jeopardizing a deal or your health. The British spelling jeopardize is not used in American writing. Usually it takes a direct object, and you can say jeopardize something by doing something.

distinctions.note: Endanger is more physical and direct, often about life or safety; jeopardize often concerns plans, reputations, or outcomes.
Risk can be a neutral choice or a noun; jeopardize means that something valuable is actually put in danger by an action.

examples.everyday: If you stay up all night again, you will jeopardize your health before the wedding.
examples.professional: Cutting the testing phase would jeopardize the launch date and could put customer data at risk.
examples.analytical: Such an argument jeopardizes the coherence of the whole theory, since it depends on premises it cannot defend.

nuance.analogy: To jeopardize something is like pulling a loose thread in a sweater: one small move can unravel the whole thing.
nuance.etymology: From jeopardy, from Old French jeu parti, meaning an evenly divided game.
common_mistakes: Spelling it jeopardize, the British form.
Using jeopardize with a preposition, as in jeopardize on something; it takes a direct object.

core.definition: The first king of the northern kingdom of Israel after the division of the monarchy, who set up golden calves at Dan and Bethel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, 'boh'. The final syllable is reduced to 'uhm', and the middle vowel is a light 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: negative in religious contexts, since the name is linked to idolatry.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Jeroboam mainly in Bible study, history and church contexts. In wine circles 'jeroboam' also means a large bottle holding about three liters (four regular bottles), which is a different sense that some Americans will think of.

distinctions.note: Jeroboam II was a later king of Israel, and the name is used for both, so specify the number when it matters.

examples.everyday: My pastor said Jeroboam led the people into idol worship, so we talked about why it mattered.
examples.professional: In the sermon outline, Jeroboam stands for the political use of religion, which is the lesson we want the congregation to take away.
examples.analytical: The Deuteronomistic narrative presents Jeroboam as the archetype of religious apostasy, and the phrase 'the sin of Jeroboam' becomes a standard evaluation of later kings.

nuance.analogy: Like a founder who builds a second house of worship and makes it a rival to the first: the name becomes a warning.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Yarov'am, probably meaning 'the people increase' or 'may the people be many'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable 'bo' as a full 'bow' sound.
Confusing the king with the wine bottle sense in religious contexts.
nuance.biblical_note: Jeroboam, son of Nebat, was the first king of the northern kingdom after the split from Judah. He made two golden calves, set up at Bethel and Dan, so that the people would not return to Jerusalem to worship (1 Kings 12:28-29). The Bible repeatedly judges later kings by 'the sin of Jeroboam' (1 Kings 15:26), and his story is told in 1 Kings 11:26-14:20.

senses.definition: The improper or corrupt act or conduct of public or official business for the sake of private gain.

core.definition: Corrupt use of a public office or position for private gain, often by giving jobs or favors to friends and supporters.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The last syllable is a reduced uh-ree, not a long e in the middle of the word.

nuance.connotation: negative; it implies dishonest use of public power.
nuance.usage_note: Jobbery is a rare, formal word found mainly in older political writing and British usage. Americans usually say patronage for handing out government jobs to supporters, or corruption, graft or cronyism for illegal profit. In conversation, corruption or cronyism is the natural choice.

distinctions.note: Patronage is the legal giving of government jobs to supporters, while jobbery implies the same practice is corrupt.
Corruption is the general word for dishonest use of power; jobbery is narrower and more old-fashioned.

examples.everyday: Neighbors were angry about the jobbery at city hall, where the mayor's friends got the contracts.
examples.professional: The audit memo flagged jobbery in the hiring of county contractors and recommended a clear review process.
examples.analytical: Critics of the spoils system described its patronage as jobbery that corroded public trust in government.

nuance.etymology: From the old verb job, meaning to trade in public office for private gain, plus -ery.
common_mistakes: Using jobbery for an ordinary job or work; the word means corrupt dealing with public positions.
Pronouncing the first syllable as 'joe' rather than JAHB.

core.definition: The father of Jeshua (Joshua), the high priest who returned from Babylonian exile and helped rebuild the Jerusalem temple.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, JOH. The middle syllable -zuh- is a quick schwa, and the final -dak rhymes with back.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a biblical name with no strong positive or negative association in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say Jozadak outside Bible study, church history or scholarly discussions of the postexilic period. Bible translations vary: the Book of Ezra uses Jozadak, while Haggai and Zechariah use the form Jehozadak. If you hear the name in a sermon, it is a reference to the priestly line.

distinctions.note: Jehozadak is the form used in Haggai and Zechariah, and Jozadak is the shorter form used in Ezra; both refer to the same man.

examples.everyday: During our Bible study we got stuck on a name, Jozadak, and had to look up who he was.
examples.professional: In the church history lecture, I noted that Jozadak's line produced the high priests of the restoration period.
examples.analytical: The genealogy in Ezra identifies Jeshua as the son of Jozadak, linking the restored priesthood to the exile.

nuance.analogy: Jozadak is like the grandfather in a family history book: you may not know his story, but he connects a major figure to the earlier generations.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Yehotsadaq, meaning the LORD is righteous.
common_mistakes: Placing the stress on the last syllable, as joh-zuh-DAK, instead of the first.
Confusing Jozadak with Jehozadak, which is a different spelling used in other books for the same person.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the name is Yehotsadaq, meaning the LORD is righteous. Jozadak is named in Ezra 3:2 as the father of Jeshua, who led the priests when the altar was rebuilt after the return from exile. He also appears in 1 Chronicles 6:15 as one of the priestly line taken into exile. The name shows the priestly family's continuity through the exile into the restoration period.

senses.definition: In a languid manner, without force or effort, in a manner requiring little energy or exertion.
senses.example: He languidly waved his limp wrist, glad to see us, but not wanting to expend the energy to let us know that.

core.definition: In a slow, relaxed way that shows little energy or effort.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LANG. The -ly ending is a clear ee sound, so do not reduce it to a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, often with a relaxed or slightly dreamy tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use languidly in descriptive writing and storytelling, for example about someone stretching out on a porch. It is not common in quick speech but is natural in narratives. It usually describes a calm, unhurried action rather than a worrying weakness.

distinctions.note: Slowly describes speed, while languidly describes a relaxed, low-energy manner that can be pleasant or tired.
Lazily often suggests avoiding work, while languidly describes a graceful, unhurried motion without judgment.

examples.everyday: The cat stretched out languidly in the sun, not moving at all when we walked past.
examples.professional: During the video call, she waved languidly at the slides, as if the meeting was already over.
examples.analytical: The poem's speaker moves languidly through the garden, and the slow rhythm mirrors his emotional exhaustion.

nuance.analogy: Moving languidly is like a cat on a warm windowsill: it moves only as much as it must, and no more.
nuance.etymology: From Latin languidus (faint, weary), from languere (to be faint).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long i sound in the first syllable, when it is LANG.
Using it for quick, energetic actions, which contradicts the meaning.

senses.definition: Characterized by lassitude.
Tending to bring about lassitude.

core.definition: Causing lassitude, or marked by a tired, listless feeling; slow and low in energy.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the '-TOO-' syllable, so the word is not stressed on its first syllable. Keep the last three syllables short and quick.

nuance.connotation: Negative or descriptive; it describes a slow, draining atmosphere or mood.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare, literary word that Americans mainly find in essays, reviews or fiction. In conversation, people say 'sleepy,' 'sluggish' or 'listless.' Use it to describe a situation, a place or a mood rather than a person.

distinctions.note: Listless is common and says a person lacks energy or interest; lassitudinous is formal and describes the atmosphere or cause.
Lethargic suggests a sluggish, sleepy state, often in a medical sense; lassitudinous is more poetic.

examples.everyday: The August heat made the whole afternoon feel lassitudinous, so we just sat on the porch.
examples.professional: The lassitudinous tone of the status update worried the managers, so they asked for a new plan.
examples.analytical: Melville's lassitudinous prose draws the reader into the stillness of the scene and resists any sense of progress.

nuance.analogy: Like a ceiling fan that barely turns on a hot summer afternoon.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'lassitude' with the adjective suffix '-ous'.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable, such as 'lass-ih-tood-ih-nus', which makes the word sound clumsy.
Using it for a person's feelings in everyday speech; 'listless' is more natural.
Misspelling it with a single 's' or a missing 'i'.

lassitudinous.etymology: From Latin *lassitūdō* + *-ous*, from oblique stem of Latin *lassitūdō*, from *lassus* + *-tūdō*.

senses.definition: Argumentative or combative.
Of or relating to litigation.
Inclined to engage in lawsuits.

core.definition: Inclined to bring lawsuits or to settle disputes by going to court, rather than by compromise.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TIJ, and the final syllables are reduced to a quick 'us'. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or pronounce the ending as 'ee-us'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone litigious suggests they are quarrelsome and too quick to sue, which many people see as unpleasant or unreasonable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in discussions of business, law, or social conflict, such as 'We live in a litigious society.' It sounds formal in conversation, and saying it about a specific neighbor or colleague can seem harsh. The everyday alternative is 'quick to sue' or 'always suing people.'

distinctions.note: Contentious describes someone who argues or fights in general, while litigious specifically refers to taking disputes to court.
Combative describes a personal style of fighting or arguing, but litigious is limited to the legal process of lawsuits.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is so litigious that he threatened to sue over a tree branch hanging into his yard.
examples.professional: Our legal team advised caution because the client's supplier has a reputation for being very litigious.
examples.analytical: Scholars often argue that a litigious culture can transform moral disputes into questions of legal entitlement rather than mutual responsibility.

nuance.analogy: A litigious person is like a driver who reaches for the horn and the brakes at the first disagreement, except the tool is a courtroom.
nuance.etymology: From Latin litigiosus, from litigium, meaning strife or lawsuit, from litigare, to dispute at law.
common_mistakes: Confusing litigious with litigation, which is the noun for the lawsuit itself.
Saying 'litigious' for a person who is simply argumentative in a conversation, when the word specifically concerns lawsuits.
nuance.biblical_note: Paul addresses lawsuits among believers in 1 Corinthians 6:1-8, criticizing Christians who take disputes before secular courts rather than settling them within the community. Jesus also counsels settling with an accuser quickly in Matthew 5:25-26, which many readers take as a call toward reconciliation over litigation.

senses.definition: A state resembling deadlock in which various computational processes are constantly changing but never reach a point where any of them can proceed.
To enter a state of livelock.

core.definition: A state in which processes keep changing in response to each other but never make progress, so none of them can finish.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and LIVE is pronounced with a long i like 'alive', not a short i like 'give'. The second syllable is weak but the vowel is the open 'ah' of cot, not 'aw'.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Used mainly by software engineers, operating-system and distributed-systems people, and in concurrency courses. Americans say it as a noun ('a livelock') or a verb ('the two services livelocked'). Outside computing it is rarely used, but people sometimes borrow it for stalemates in meetings or traffic.

distinctions.note: In a deadlock, processes are blocked and wait forever; in a livelock, they are active and keep responding, but still make no progress.
Starvation means one process never gets a resource it needs, while livelock involves all the processes actively retrying and yielding.

collocations: a livelock between two retry loops

examples.everyday: My laptop froze because two background apps kept undoing each other's changes, like a livelock.
examples.professional: The team traced the outage to a livelock between the two retry handlers, so we added random backoff.
examples.analytical: A livelock shows that a system can be fully active and still fail, because activity alone does not guarantee progress.

nuance.analogy: Two people in a narrow hallway keep stepping aside in the same direction, each mirroring the other, so both keep moving and neither gets past.
nuance.etymology: Formed in computing on the model of deadlock, with live suggesting that the processes are still active.
common_mistakes: Saying the vowel of 'live' as in 'give' (/lɪv/) instead of the long i of 'alive'.
Confusing livelock with deadlock; in a livelock the processes are still running.

senses.definition: Initialism of large language model.
Initialism of logic learning machine.
Initialism of licensed lay minister.
Initialism of local linear model.

core.definition: Abbreviation for large language model, an AI system trained on huge amounts of text to understand and generate language.

pronunciation.tip: Say the three letters separately, with the main stress on the final EM. Do not say it as one word like 'ell-lem'.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American tech and business meetings, people say the letters one by one and use 'an LLM' with the article 'an', because it starts with the sound of 'el'. It is used more widely now, including by non-specialists, but it is still jargon in casual talk. Say 'large language model' when you need to explain it to a general audience.

distinctions.note: A chatbot is a product or interface for conversation; it may be built on an LLM, but the LLM is the model underneath.
A neural network is the broad family of models; an LLM is a very large language-focused kind of neural network.

examples.everyday: I asked an LLM to help me plan a dinner menu for friends.
examples.professional: In our team meeting, we compared three LLM options for the customer support tool.
examples.analytical: Whether an LLM understands language or only predicts statistical patterns is a central question in the philosophy of mind.

nuance.analogy: An LLM is like a very well-read assistant who has absorbed millions of books but still needs careful checking before you trust a fact.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of large language model.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a LLM' instead of 'an LLM'.
Pronouncing it as a single word, like 'ell-lem'.

conversation.text: Let's prototype the classifier with an LLM first and only train a custom model if the costs don't work out.
The LLM call is the slowest step in the pipeline, so we cache responses to repeated questions.
LLM outputs vary between runs, so report results averaged over several samples.

senses.definition: Any of the grasshoppers, often polyphenic and usually swarming, in the family Acrididae that are very destructive to crops and other vegetation, especially migratory locusts (Locusta migratoria).
Any of various often leguminous trees and shrubs, especially of the genera Robinia and Gleditsia; locust tree.
A cicada.
Anything or anyone considered a nuisance or plague.
A fruit or pod of a carob tree.
To come in a swarm.

core.definition: A grasshopper that often swarms in huge numbers and destroys crops and other plants.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, LOH. The second syllable is a reduced vowel, so say 'kust', not 'cuss' or 'kos'.

nuance.connotation: Negative when it means a crop-destroying swarm, and it is strongly associated with plagues.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, locust often means the periodical cicada, such as the 17-year locusts, which are not true locusts. Americans also use locust for the black locust tree. In agriculture and news reports, locust means the migratory grasshopper that swarms.

distinctions.note: Grasshopper is the general word, while locust usually refers to species that can form swarms and migrate in large numbers.
Cicadas are not true locusts, but Americans often call periodical cicadas locusts.

examples.everyday: The 17-year locusts are finally out, so the trees are loud every evening.
examples.professional: The crop reports show locust damage across the farm belt this season.
examples.analytical: The plague of locusts in Exodus is described as covering the land and eating what the hail had left.

nuance.analogy: A locust swarm is like a wind of hungry bodies that strips a field in a single afternoon.
nuance.etymology: From Latin locusta, grasshopper or locust.
common_mistakes: Calling any grasshopper a locust, when the word applies mainly to swarming species.
Stressing the second syllable, saying lo-CUST.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word is 'arbeh (אַרְבֶּה), meaning locust, and the Greek is akris (ἀκρίς), meaning locust or grasshopper. In the RSV, the plague of locusts in Exodus 10:4-19 shows locusts as a divine judgment that devours crops. Joel 1:4 and Joel 2:25 describe locusts as destroyers of the harvest that God promises to restore. Matthew 3:4 says John the Baptist ate locusts and wild honey in the wilderness.

locust.etymology: Middle English *locuste*, *locust*, from Anglo-Norman *locuste*, Middle French *locuste*, and their source, Latin *locusta* (“locust, crustacean, lobster”).

senses.definition: To cease to have (something) in one's possession or capability.
senses.example: If you lose that ten-pound note, you'll be sorry.

senses.definition: To have (an organ) removed from one's body, especially by accident.
senses.example: Johnny lost a tooth, but kept it for the tooth fairy.

senses.definition: To shed (weight).
senses.example: I’ve lost five pounds this week.

senses.definition: To experience the death of (someone to whom one has an attachment, such as a relative or friend).
senses.example: She lost all her sons in the war.

senses.definition: To pay or owe (some wager) due from an unsuccessful bet or gamble.
senses.example: Frank had lost $500 staying in Vegas.

senses.definition: To be deprived of (some right or privileged access to something).
senses.example: Users who engage in disruptive behavior may lose their accounts.

senses.definition: To wander from; to miss, so as not to be able to find; to go astray from.
senses.example: I lost my way in the forest.

senses.definition: To become a defeated competitor in (a game, competition, trial, etc).
senses.example: We lost the football match.

senses.definition: To be defeated.
senses.example: The team scored four goals but still managed to lose.

senses.definition: To be unable to follow or trace (somebody or something) any longer.
senses.example: The policeman lost the robber he was chasing.

senses.definition: To cause (somebody) to be unable to follow or trace one any longer.
senses.example: lose the cops

senses.definition: To cease exhibiting; to overcome (a behavior or emotion).
To shed, remove, discard, or eliminate.
senses.example: When we get into the building, please lose the hat.

senses.definition: Of a clock, to run slower than expected.
senses.example: My watch loses five minutes a week.

senses.definition: To cause (someone) the loss of something; to deprive of.
To fail to catch with the mind or senses; to miss.
senses.example: She moved out of hearing and I lost the end of the sentence.

core.definition: To no longer have something you had, or to be unable to find it, keep it, or win it.

pronunciation.tip: Say it with a z sound at the end, not an s, and keep the vowel long and tense. Do not confuse it with loose, which is pronounced with an s sound.

nuance.connotation: neutral to negative, depending on whether the loss is important or trivial.
nuance.usage_note: Lose is one of the most common verbs in American English, used for everyday items, games, weight, and emotions. Americans say I lost my keys in everyday talk and I lost the game in sports. The past tense and past participle are both lost.

distinctions.note: Lose means you no longer have something or lost a contest, while miss usually means you failed to catch, attend, or notice something.
Misplace means you put something somewhere and cannot remember where, while lose means it is gone or you cannot find it.

examples.everyday: I can never remember where I put my phone, so I lose it all the time.
examples.professional: If we keep missing deadlines, we will lose the client's trust.
examples.analytical: Descartes asks what we lose when we doubt everything, and whether certainty can be recovered.

nuance.analogy: Losing something is like a coin slipping out of your pocket; it is no longer with you, even if you might find it later.
